newsitem.title: UK: Owner-row halts London firm's Gandhi letters sale.
newsitem.headline: Owner-row halts London firm's Gandhi letters sale.

text.p: A London auction house said on Tuesday it had cancelled the sale of a collection of writings by India's revered independence leader Mahatma Gandhi after their ownership came into dispute. Gandhi's former secretary, Venkataraman Kalyanam, who kept the papers at his Madras home for nearly 50 years, had offered them for sale to raise money for a Hindu charity.
But the Indian government intervened last month, saying the valuable collection should be preserved for the nation and arguing that it belonged to the trust that safeguards Gandhi memorabilia.

"We have pulled out of the sale, it is no longer anything to do with us," said a spokeswoman for the auctioneers Phillips, which had said the sale would raise up to one million pounds ($1.65 million).
The auction had been scheduled for November 14.
The papers were written in the months before Gandhi was assassinated by a Hindu fanatic in 1948. Kalyanam, who is in his 70's, says that Gandhi had asked him to keep them.
There are some 450 pages in Gandhi's crabbed handwriting, some written on the backs of used envelopes to save paper.

They include letters to Britain's wartime prime minister, Winston Churchill, and Louis Mountbatten, the last British viceroy of India revealing Gandhi's anxieties in the run-up to India's independence in 1947.

Gandhi, a devout Hindu who led 350 million Indians in a non-violent campaign against British rule, also writes of his great distress at sectarian Moslem-Hindu violence that swept India following partition.
Phillips said it had been asked to keep the papers until lawyers resolved the question of who owned them.
"All the parties have agreed to that," the spokeswoman said.
India's High Commission (embassy) in London had played a key role in halting the sale after learning about it in the British media last month and relaying the news back to India.
"The papers should be returned to India, they should not be sold," said a High Commission spokesman.
